source: Ioannidis (2005) Why most published research findings are false
finding: A formal model: the chance a significant finding is true (PPV) depends on power, the prior odds R that a tested relation is true, and bias u. Low prior odds and low power make most positive claims false.
numbers: Table 4: power 0.80, R 1:1, u 0.10 gives PPV 0.85. Power 0.20, R 1:5, u 0.80 gives 0.17. Exploratory epidemiology, power 0.20, R 1:10, u 0.30 gives 0.12. Massive discovery testing, R 1:1000, u 0.80 gives 0.0010.
quote: Why Most Published Research Findings Are False
limits: Theoretical; inputs R and u are assumed, not measured. Later critics (e.g. Jager and Leek 2014) estimated lower false rates.
agent_relevance: Agent rule for G3: a surprising positive result from many tries (many candidate thoughts, many searches) has low odds of being true. Weight by prior and by number of tries.

source: Ioannidis (2005) Why most published research findings are false (corollaries)
finding: Six corollaries: smaller studies, smaller effects, more tested relationships, more design flexibility, more financial or other interest, and more teams chasing one question all lower PPV.
numbers: Hot fields with many teams: the first claim of significance by any team is often not a real effect; early results often contradicted by later larger studies.
limits: Argument by modelling, not a measured rate.
agent_relevance: Supports a cross-check operator: re-derive a claim by an independent route before accepting it.

source: Errington et al. (2021) Challenges for assessing replicability in preclinical cancer biology (Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology)
finding: The project planned to repeat 193 experiments from 53 high-impact papers but could only repeat 50 experiments from 23 papers, because papers lacked the data and method detail needed.
numbers: Raw data or effect-size data public for 4 of 193 experiments (2%); raw data shared for 31 (16%); nothing shared for 131 (68%). Zero of 193 experiments were described fully enough to design a protocol. Authors extremely or very helpful for 41%, minimally 9%, not helpful or no reply 32%. 67% of peer-reviewed protocols needed changes; only 41% of those changes could be done.
limits: This paper reports barriers, not the replication outcomes (companion paper).
agent_relevance: A claim whose method or numbers cannot be recovered is not checkable. Agent should log exact inputs and steps so its own chain can be re-run.

source: Open Science Collaboration (2015) Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science
finding: 100 studies from three psychology journals were repeated. Far fewer were significant on replication, and effects shrank by about half.
numbers: Original significant: 97 of 100. Replications significant: 36 percent. Mean effect size r about 0.40 originally, about 0.20 in replications. (from memory, not opened)
limits: Not opened this session. Replication success has no single definition; Gilbert et al. 2016 challenged the reading.
agent_relevance: Prior for a published effect without independent replication should be shrunk; effect sizes roughly halved.

source: Camerer et al. (2018) Evaluating the replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science 2010-2015
finding: 21 high-profile social science experiments were repeated with samples about five times larger. Most replicated in direction but effects were smaller.
numbers: 13 of 21 (62 percent) significant in the same direction. Replication effect size about 50 percent of the original on average. (from memory, not opened)
limits: Not opened this session. Prediction markets and surveys forecast outcomes well.
agent_relevance: A calibrated replicate-or-not forecast by peers is informative; the agent can make such a forecast about its own claims.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2: variation in replicability across samples and settings
finding: 28 classic findings were run at many sites worldwide. About half replicated. Variation across sample and setting was small compared with the gap between effects.
numbers: About 14 of 28 findings replicated at p<.05; about 15,000 participants over 36 sites. (from memory, not opened; download failed)
limits: Not opened. The hidden-moderator excuse is weak: heterogeneity was small.
agent_relevance: Do not explain away a failed check by 'context differs' without evidence of a moderator.

source: Simmons, Nelson, Simonsohn (2011) False-positive psychology
finding: Undisclosed analytic flexibility (outcome choice, stopping rule, covariates, dropping conditions) can make almost anything significant.
numbers: Combined flexibility pushed the false-positive rate to about 61 percent at p<.05. (from memory, not opened)
limits: Not opened this session. Simulations plus two demonstration experiments.
agent_relevance: The agent's own choices (which thought to keep, when to stop) are a forking path. Fix the scoring rule before looking, and report all branches tried.

source: Franco, Malhotra, Simonovits (2014) Publication bias in the social sciences: unlocking the file drawer
finding: Tracking 221 funded studies, null results were far less likely to be written up or published than strong results.
numbers: About 65 percent of strong-result studies written up versus about 20 percent of null studies (approximate, from memory, not opened).
limits: Not opened; exact percentages need checking before citing.
agent_relevance: Knowledge learned from literature over-represents positive findings; the agent should discount typical claims.

source: Button et al. (2013) Power failure: why small sample size undermines the reliability of neuroscience
finding: Meta-analyses in neuroscience showed very low statistical power, which inflates significant effects and lowers PPV.
numbers: Median statistical power about 21 percent across 49 meta-analyses (from memory, not opened).
limits: Not opened this session.
agent_relevance: A small test set cannot support a claim of improvement; use enough items and report intervals.

source: Benjamin et al. (2018) Redefine statistical significance
finding: Proposed lowering the default threshold for new claims from p<.05 to p<.005. Rival view (Lakens et al. 2018): justify alpha per study. Another (Amrhein 2019): drop the dichotomy.
numbers: p<.05 corresponds to Bayes factors of roughly 3 to 5 at best; p<.005 to about 14 to 26 (from memory, not opened; download failed).
limits: Not opened. The three proposals disagree and no experiment decides between them.
agent_relevance: Report effect size and uncertainty, not a single pass/fail; demand stronger evidence for novel claims.

source: Siegel, Kapoor, Nadgir, Stroebl, Narayanan (2024; v2 2026) CORE-Bench: computational reproducibility agent benchmark
finding: 270 tasks from 90 papers (CS, social science, medicine) test whether agents can reproduce results from supplied code and data. Best agent reached 21 percent on the hardest level.
numbers: Best accuracy 21 percent on the hardest level with GPT-4o. Survey table in paper: ML reproducibility challenge 2022, 18 of 28 papers with code and data fully reproduced; economics (Gertler 2018) 128 of 203; computer systems (Collberg 2016) 311 of 601.
limits: Original models were GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini; newer agents score higher (later versions of the paper).
agent_relevance: Even with code and data, reproduction is fragile. Agent should run the check, not trust reported numbers.

source: Chan et al. (2025) MLE-bench
finding: 75 Kaggle competitions. Best setup (o1-preview with AIDE) got at least bronze in 16.9 percent. More attempts help a lot.
numbers: pass@1 16.9 percent; pass@8 34.1 percent for o1-preview. GPT-4o 8.7 percent at 24 hours versus 11.8 percent with more time. Authors judge contamination effects minimal.
limits: Public Kaggle tasks may leak into training.
agent_relevance: Best-of-k raises success only if the selector is reliable. Report pass@1 and pass@k separately.

source: Starace et al. (2025) PaperBench: evaluating AI's ability to replicate AI research
finding: Agents replicate 20 ICML 2024 papers from scratch, graded by 8,316 rubric items with an LLM judge. Humans still beat agents on a subset.
numbers: Best agent Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New): 21.0 percent. On a 3-paper subset, ML PhDs (best of 3, 48 hours) 41.4 percent versus o1 26.6 percent. Code-Dev variant: o1 43.4 percent.
limits: Partial-credit rubric; LLM judge imperfect; rules forbid using the authors' code.
agent_relevance: Replication from method text alone is hard. Decompose into checkable sub-goals.

source: Hu et al. (2025) REPRO-BENCH
finding: 112 social science papers; agents must score the reproducibility of a paper from PDF plus reproduction package. Existing agents did worse than chance.
numbers: Best existing agent 21.4 percent accuracy versus 25 percent random on a 4-level score. REPRO-AGENT 36.6 percent, a 71 percent relative gain.
limits: Small set; coarse 4-level scale.
agent_relevance: Judging a study is harder than rerunning it. The agent should not assume it can grade evidence by reading alone.

source: Baumann et al. (2025) Large Language Model Hacking: hidden risks of using LLMs for text annotation
finding: Analogue of p-hacking: choice of model, prompt and settings changes downstream statistical conclusions. 13 million labels, 18 LLMs, 2,361 hypotheses from 37 tasks in 21 studies.
numbers: Wrong conclusions in about 31 percent of hypotheses for state-of-the-art LLMs and about half for small models. With paraphrases: false positives feasible for 94.4 percent of null hypotheses, true effects hidden in 98.1 percent, sign reversed in 68.3 percent of true differences. Human-label correction gives Type I about 10 percent but raises Type II by up to 60 points. With 1,000 human labels risk is still about 20 percent.
quote: with just a handful of prompt paraphrases, virtually anything can be presented as statistically significant
limits: Annotation tasks, not reasoning; risk falls as true effects grow.
agent_relevance: Direct G3 evidence: prompt and model choice are researcher degrees of freedom. Pre-fix prompts, run paraphrases, distrust results near the threshold.

source: Nguyen et al. (2026) ReplicatorBench
finding: Benchmark with real replication outcomes from the Center for Open Science. Agents design and run code well but are weaker at data retrieval and at judging if replication succeeded.
numbers: GPT-5 best on binary replication outcome, about 10 percent net gain over o3; GPT-5-mini macro F1 47.86. Interpretation-stage LLMEval: GPT-5 91.26, o3 94.54, GPT-4o 82.25, GPT-5-mini 87.02 (as in the section read).
limits: LLM-judged stages; model-to-score mapping taken from the text read.
agent_relevance: Stage-wise scoring shows where a pipeline breaks; add a retrieve-and-verify step.

source: Saynova et al. (2025) Identifying non-replicable social science studies with language models
finding: LLMs simulate participants in 14 studies replicated in Many Labs 2 (9 successful, 5 failed) and judge if the original effect holds. Low sampling variance biases effect sizes.
numbers: F1 up to 77 percent Mistral 7B, 67 percent GPT-4o and Llama 3 8B, 55 percent Qwen2 7B. GPT-4o by temperature: 0.1 F1 0.50, 0.5 F1 0.67, 1.0 F1 0.36; only 10 to 11 of 14 studies gave usable estimates.
limits: Only 14 studies; 9 of 14 base rate makes F1 unstable.
agent_relevance: Silicon samples are not independent replications; do not count simulated people as evidence.

source: Kohler et al. (2026) Read the paper, write the code: agentic reproduction of social-science results
finding: Agents given only methods text and data (not code) re-implement analyses for 48 human-verified reproducible papers. Largely successful but varies by model and scaffold; failures come from agent errors and paper underspecification.
numbers: Top three agents: sign agreement about 85 to 91 percent. Best agent within 1.96 original SE over 80 percent of the time. Best: GPT-5.4 with OpenCode scaffold.
limits: Only papers already known reproducible.
agent_relevance: Underspecified methods cause failures; write methods that a stranger could rerun.

source: Alizadeh et al. (2026) AI coding agents can reproduce social science findings (SocSci-Repro-Bench)
finding: 221 tasks. Claude Code far outperformed Codex. Adding the paper PDF helps a little but makes agents echo the paper's number even when reproduction is impossible.
numbers: Task accuracy 93.4 vs 62.1 percent; paper level 78.0 vs 35.8 percent. With PDF: 94.5 and 65.4 percent. On non-reproducible tasks PDF access cut accuracy from 100 to 63.3 percent (Claude Code) and 100 to 90.0 percent (Codex).
limits: Two agents only.
agent_relevance: Anchoring on the expected answer beats the evidence at hand. The agent must be able to say cannot be reproduced.

source: Alizadeh et al. (2026) Confirmatory prompt nudging (section 2.4 of the same paper)
finding: Told to explore alternative specifications that align with reported results (sycophancy nudge), agents scored higher overall but worse on impossible tasks.
numbers: Task accuracy Claude Code 93.4 to 94.1 percent; Codex 62.1 to 74.1 percent. Codex task failure rate fell 17.8 to 0.5 percent. Accuracy on non-reproducible tasks declined substantially (exact values not extracted).
limits: Two agents; exact decline not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Goal pressure increases persistence but pushes toward specification search. Keep the success criterion separate from instructions to try variants.

source: Holtdirk et al. (2026) Automated reproducibility assessments in social and behavioral sciences using LLMs
finding: An LLM pipeline reanalysed 180 studies with predefined claims. Direction usually recovered; effect size seldom exact.
numbers: Same qualitative conclusion in 80 percent; effect within plus or minus 0.05 Cohen's d in 24 percent, within 0.20 in 50 percent. Human-reanalysis subset: 95 percent LLM vs 83 percent human same conclusion; exact effect recovery 40 vs 28 percent. 11 studies had no viable estimate. Reproduction with source data beat reproduction with replication data.
limits: Claims predefined; tolerance choice drives the headline number.
agent_relevance: Report direction with confidence, treat point estimates as loose.

source: Park, Schoenegger, Zhu (2023) Diminished diversity-of-thought in a standard LLM
finding: Model answers are less varied than human ones, so simulated samples understate variance and distort effect sizes.
numbers: No figures extracted; cited by Saynova et al. for the low-variance mechanism.
limits: Only the opening text was read.
agent_relevance: Repeated samples from one model are not independent; self-consistency votes overstate agreement.

source: Errington et al. (2021) Investigating the replicability of preclinical cancer biology
finding: Companion paper with outcomes of the 50 repeated experiments: effects were much smaller than originals.
numbers: Median effect size about 85 percent smaller than original (from memory, not opened).
limits: Not opened; check before citing.
agent_relevance: Same shrinkage as in psychology: expect large drops.

source: Gilbert, King, Pettigrew, Wilson (2016) Comment on Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science
finding: Rival reading: error, power and fidelity of replications mean the true replication rate may be near 100 percent. The Open Science Collaboration disagreed in a reply.
numbers: Claimed original effects lay inside the replication 95 percent interval about 75 percent of the time (from memory, not opened).
limits: Not opened; contested.
agent_relevance: One pass/fail replication is a noisy measure; weigh several.

source: Hardwicke et al. (2018, 2021) and Obels et al. (2020) analytic reproducibility in psychology, as listed in CORE-Bench Table 1
finding: Even with data and code shared, many psychology papers could not be reproduced.
numbers: Table rows: Hardwicke 2021: 25 studies, 16; Obels 2020: 36 studies, 15; Hardwicke 2018: 35 studies, 13. Second number per row is as printed; the table header was garbled, so its meaning (reproduced or reviewed) is unverified.
limits: Column meaning unverified.
agent_relevance: Plan checks into the loop; base rate of non-reproduction is high.
